guide.title: Shock & Hemorrhage
guide.lead: Shock is not a BP number. It's when tissues don't get enough oxygen. Catch it early from the anxiety, the fast pulse and the cold, pale skin; hypotension is late. In trauma, stop the bleeding first.

sections.title: Four kinds of shock
rows: Flat neck veins, cold and pale
Warm skin early; rash, fever, wheeze
Raised JVP, absent breath sounds, muffled heart sounds

steps.title: Tourniquet
steps.text: 5–7 cm (2–3 inches) above the wound, not over a joint. Tighten until the bleeding stops; note the time.

steps.title: Still bleeding?
steps.text: A second tourniquet above the first.

steps.title: Junctional wound (groin, armpit, neck)
steps.text: Pack with hemostatic gauze and press.

steps.title: Tranexamic acid
steps.text: Within 3 hours of injury, per protocol.

sections.title: How much blood is gone?
rows: Tachycardia, anxiety, narrowed pulse pressure; BP maintained
Lethargic, very low BP: about to arrest

sections.title: Every shock patient
items: Keep warm: cold, acid and clotting failure feed each other
Pelvic binder for suspected pelvic fracture with shock
Rapid transport to the right centre; fluids en route (4.11)

quiz.q: Which picture fits class III hemorrhage?
Fall from a ladder: confused, cold and clammy, HR 124, BP 88/60, deformed femur. First priority?
options: Treat shock: oxygen, keep warm, splint, rapid transport to a trauma centre with fluids en route
Elevate the legs and wait for ALS
quiz.explanation: A femur fracture can hide a lot of blood.

quiz.q: Spinal injury at T3: BP 82, HR 52, warm, flushed skin. Type of shock?
quiz.explanation: Bradycardia and warm skin are the clues. Still look for bleeding.

quiz.q: Where should a limb tourniquet go?
options: 5–7 cm above the wound, not over a joint
quiz.explanation: Tighten until the bleeding stops; note the time.
1 g IV over 10 minutes, per protocol.

quiz.q: Hypotension, raised neck veins and muffled heart sounds after a stab wound:
Why keep a bleeding patient warm?
options: Cold worsens clotting failure and acidosis
quiz.explanation: Hypothermia, acidosis and coagulopathy feed each other.

quiz.q: Shock with hives, wheeze and swelling after a bee sting. First drug?
quiz.explanation: 0.01 mg/kg, maximum 0.5 mg; repeat after 5 minutes if needed.

quiz.q: Hypotension, absent breath sounds on one side and distended neck veins after chest trauma:

flashcards.question: Why hypotension is a late sign
flashcards.answer: Compensation keeps BP up until large losses (class III, 31–40%).

flashcards.question: First measurable sign of compensated shock
Class II vs class III hemorrhage
flashcards.answer: II (15–30%): tachycardia, narrowed pulse pressure, BP maintained. III (31–40%): hypotension, confusion, marked tachycardia.

flashcards.question: Controlling limb bleeding
flashcards.answer: Direct pressure; tourniquet 5–7 cm above the wound for life-threatening limb bleeding; hemostatic packing for junctional wounds.

flashcards.question: Permissive hypotension
flashcards.answer: In hemorrhage without head injury: small fluid boluses to a radial pulse or systolic 80–90 mmHg, so clots aren't disrupted.

flashcards.question: Skin in compensated shock
flashcards.answer: Pale, cool, clammy: vasoconstriction and sympathetic sweating.

flashcards.question: Why keep a shock patient warm?
flashcards.answer: Cold worsens clotting failure and acidosis, especially in hemorrhage.

critical.scenario: A worker fell onto rebar. Bright red blood spurts from the upper thigh. Pale, sweaty, agitated; HR about 130, no radial pulse.
critical.question: First intervention?

options.t: Control the bleeding: direct pressure, then a tourniquet 5–7 cm above the wound
Oxygen and a full set of vital signs
options.f: He'll bleed out while you measure.
Fluid can't replace blood still pouring out.

options.t: Splint and move to the ambulance

critical.explanation: Then oxygen, warmth, permissive fluids and rapid transport to a trauma centre.
critical.kpi: Prioritises haemorrhage control over other interventions in exsanguinating extremity injury

critical.scenario: An 82-year-old has black stools for 3 days and coffee-ground vomit. Confused, pale, cool. HR 112, BP 90/68. Hospital 25 minutes away.
critical.question: Best plan?

options.t: Oxygen to target, IV access en route, small fluid boluses to keep systolic 80–90 mmHg, keep warm, transport
Large boluses to a normal BP

options.f: She needs a hospital to stop the bleeding.

critical.explanation: Reassess mental status and BP after each bolus.
critical.kpi: Applies permissive hypotension principle in non-traumatic haemorrhagic shock

critical.scenario: A 60-year-old with anterior STEMI: HR 118, BP 88/60, SpO₂ 91%, crackles at both bases and pink frothy sputum. Your partner wants a full fluid bolus.
critical.question: Fluid plan?

options.t: No large bolus: this is cardiogenic shock with pulmonary edema; at most a small cautious challenge on medical direction, and go to PCI

options.f: Not with a systolic below 90 mmHg.

critical.explanation: The treatment is opening the artery; vasopressors are ALS.
critical.kpi: Identifies cardiogenic shock and avoids fluid overload in the setting of pulmonary oedema
